neighbor_comparisons.actual_core_read: Read whole as a degree-versus-order relation for subdivided expanders: with k_n = ceil((n/log^d n)^{1/(d-1)}) and n_s = n + (3n/2)(k_n - 1), there are C_1, C_2, N_3 depending on d with C_1 n_s^{1-1/d} log n_s <= n <= C_2 n_s^{1-1/d} log n_s for every n >= N_3. The proof sets x_n, squeezes k_n between x_n and 2x_n, bounds n_s between (3/4)n x_n and 3n x_n, records eq:nN-two-sided, inverts it to eq:N-vs-nN, bounds log n against log n_s in eq:logsbound, and assembles C_1 = ((d-1)/(2d-1))(1/3)^{1-1/d} and C_2 = (4/3)^{1-1/d}.
neighbor_comparisons.reason_target_distinct: The neighbour compares the number of vertices n before subdivision with the order n_s after uniform subdivision by paths of length k_n, and asks only for two-sided polynomial-logarithmic constants in d. Exercise 6.88 measures an anchored edge-expansion constant of a random subdivision of a binary tree under a law nu with no exponential tail, and asks whether that constant is 0 a.s. while the base tree keeps positive anchored expansion. The neighbour has no random law, no tail condition, no anchored or isoperimetric constant, no binary tree and no a.s. statement; the shared word is "subdivision" only.

neighbor_comparisons.actual_core_read: Read whole as a tail-decay estimate for a matrix-valued convolution series: for V = I(v) in G(alpha, K) with alpha < 1 and R_v^infty(t) preceq A(1+t)^{-gamma} V, the sum psi = sum v^{*n} satisfies R_psi^infty(t) preceq A(1+gamma/(delta log(1/alpha)))^gamma (1+t)^{-gamma(1-delta)} V (Id-V)^{-2} + V^{floor(gamma(1-delta)log(1+t)/log(1/alpha))+2}(Id-V)^{-2}, with a sup-norm corollary. The proof applies the earlier Proposition 4.2 with p = exp(-delta/epsilon), cuts at k_0 = floor(epsilon log(1+t)) for epsilon = gamma(1-delta)/log(1/alpha), and uses alpha^{k_0+2} <= alpha(1+t)^{-gamma(1-delta)}.
neighbor_comparisons.reason_target_distinct: This is the nearest neighbour in vocabulary: it is genuinely about exponential tails. But its object is the resolvent of a matrix-valued convolution series for a multitype Poisson branching process and its Hawkes-process application, and its content is a polynomial decay rate in t for that resolvent. Exercise 6.88 uses the failure of an exponential tail as a hypothesis about a subdivision law, and its content is the vanishing of an anchored edge-expansion constant for the random subdivision of a binary tree. The neighbour contains no graph, no subdivision, no boundary or anchored expansion and no statement about a.s. vanishing; an "exponential tail" appearing in both titles is not coverage of the exercise.
neighbor_comparisons.title: Exponential Tail Estimates for Multitype Poisson Branching Processes and Application to Hawkes Processes
neighbor_comparisons.source_work: Exponential Tail Estimates for Multitype Poisson Branching Processes and Application to Hawkes Processes

neighbor_comparisons.actual_core_read: Read whole as a path-collection lemma in induced-subdivision extremal combinatorics: for h, r >= 1, a >= 16h, G an r-expander with r >= 10^{23} h^2 Delta(G) log^3 Delta(G) and disjoint S_1..S_{2h} inside U satisfying the three stated conditions, some half of the sets carries disjoint induced paths P_{i,j} from S_i to S_j with |P_{i,j} cap U| = 2. The proof builds the paths one pair at a time, discards sets that lose too many vertices, bounds |B^{(l)}(U) cap V(P)| by 2(20 log Delta(G))^3 (l+1)^3 + 2, and keeps at least h non-overused sets.
neighbor_comparisons.reason_target_distinct: The neighbour is a structural lemma producing 2h pairwise disjoint induced paths between prescribed vertex sets in an expander, used for induced subdivision bounds. Exercise 6.88 also uses many disjoint paths, but probabilistically: the 2^n level-n-to-level-2n paths of the binary tree are weighted by i.i.d. lengths and the conclusion is a bound on the ratio of the boundary of one extended path to the sum of its edge lengths. The neighbour has no random weighting, no tail hypothesis, no boundary-to-length ratio and no binary-tree level count.
neighbor_comparisons.title: Nearly tight bounds for induced subdivisions
neighbor_comparisons.source_work: Nearly tight bounds for induced subdivisions

neighbor_comparisons.actual_core_read: Read whole as an equivalence theorem for finite ultrametric spaces: for two MCD-spaces, isometry, isomorphism of the labelled rooted representing trees T_X and T_Y, isomorphism of T_X(l_X) and T_Y(l_Y), equality of the centers of distances C(X) = C(Y) (label m2) and equality of the distance sets D(X) = D(Y) are all equivalent. The proof chains (i)<=>(ii) through Theorem rvqqbb, (ii)<=>(iii) through Proposition effrt, (iv)<=>(v) through Lemma UT2Lemma3, (i)=>(iv) from the definition of centers of distances, and closes (iv)=>(i) by induction on n + 1 = |C(X)| = |C(Y)|.
neighbor_comparisons.reason_target_distinct: The neighbour is about finite ultrametric spaces and their representing trees, which are perfect binary trees; its theorem characterises isometry of two such spaces by isomorphism of labelled rooted trees and by equality of centers of distances. Exercise 6.88 is about an infinite binary tree with a random subdivision and an anchored edge-expansion constant, i.e. about isoperimetry on a random graph, not about isometry classification of finite ultrametric spaces. The shared word "binary tree" carries no coverage; the neighbour states no expansion constant and no probability law on lengths.
